newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-BHP warns on assets sale from May 1998.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-BHP warns on assets sale from May 1998.

text.p: The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP) said on Tuesday it may sell any non-strategic assets which were not performing satisfactorily by May 1998.

"Those assets not earning a return on their capital of more than 10 percent by May 1998, and that are not considered strategic, will either fixed or sold," BHP managing director John Prescott told a business luncheon.

He said also BHP was on track to reduce the company's debt by A$4 billion by May next year. "We have reduced debt by A$2.5 billion since August last year, and we are on track to reduce debt by A$4 billion by May next year," Prescott said.
BHP aims to lift returns on all of its assets above eight percent by last May and then consider for sale all those assets not earning at least 10 percent by next May.
Prescott described the first step as "having been largely sucessful".
Prescott outlined targets for the group including better returns on equity, profits and dividends, strong cash flow and balance sheet.
He predicted BHP would become more of a gas company than an oil company and "will have more metallurgical coal".
"We will go from few metals to many metals; we will add value to our products and for our customers in new ways," he said.

Listing the group's underperforming assets, Prescott listed the steel assets at Whyalla, in South Australia, New Zealand, Newcastle and two Asian roll-forming businesses, which he said BHP intended to sell.

"All other busiensses in steel - and there are 40 of them -- are earning above eight percent return on capital," Prescott said, adding that about 20 steel operations achieved better than 15 percent return.
In minerals, a small number of coal mines and the Temco business were also below the eight percent target. "And we ahve plans in place in respect of these businesses," Prescott said.
In petroleum, the Hawaiian refinery and Bruce field in the North Sea were below target, while in the copper division, some of the North American assets were also below target.

"What I am talking about here is the underlying performance of the various businesses," Prescott said. "It does not include allowance for overheads, exploration and development costs and the other costs of growing the company. I am talking about the basic quality of the assets."

Prescott said BHP, Australia's largest listed company, was also undertaking a review to ensure that new projects delivered, although he added that it was unreasonable to expect new projects to deliver fully on start-up.
BHP suffered management turmoil earlier this month with three senior executives resigned in three days, including the head of BHP's minerals division and the petroleum chief.
BHP also revealed cost overruns at its Pilbara hot briquetted iron (HBI) project in Western Australia.

"The HBI project is particularly complex," Prescott said today. "We are concerned about cost over-runs and delays on the HBI projects, and we have in place a cross-business group review into all aspects of the management of the project, led by the executive general manager finance."
Prescott said BHP was also seeking better returns for shareholders by applying a renewed rigour in assessing potenital projects.
"We are making increasing use of cross-business group teams to assess every aspect of new projects and to challenge the assumptions underlying the proposals," he said.
BHP shares were 5.2 cents firmer at A$17.16 at 1.50 p.m. (0350 GMT) on Tuesday.
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1421
